title: Dislocated kneecap: urgent care and a safe return to activity
intro: A dislocated kneecap has slipped out of the groove at the front of the thighbone, usually toward the outside of the knee. A twist or impact can cause it, and some knee shapes make it more likely. Even when the kneecap moves back by itself, the injury needs assessment because cartilage, bone or stabilising ligaments may be damaged.

sections.heading: Recognise the injury without trying to repair it
paragraphs: Sudden pain, swelling, a popping sensation, a visible change in shape or inability to use the knee can occur. If it remains out of place, obtain emergency assessment. A rapidly swelling or deformed knee, an open wound with visible bone, heavy bleeding, or a cold, pale or numb foot also needs emergency care. Do not try to push the kneecap back, force the knee straight or walk on the injured leg. Keep the knee still and supported with padding in the position found, without forcing it up. Arrange help rather than driving yourself; call emergency services if movement or transport is unsafe. If it has returned to place, still seek prompt medical assessment.

sections.heading: Assessment checks more than the kneecap's position
paragraphs: Explain the injury, any previous episodes, locking, swelling and whether the knee has felt unstable before. The clinician checks the joint, ability to move and straighten, circulation and sensation. X-rays commonly look for fracture or displaced bone; further imaging, such as an MRI, may assess cartilage, loose fragments or ligament injury when indicated. Persistent locking or inability to straighten can matter even when the kneecap looks normal. A dislocated kneecap differs from dislocation of the main knee joint, which can seriously damage vessels and nerves; do not make that distinction yourself after a major injury. Treatment depends on the complete findings.

sections.heading: Initial treatment and decisions about surgery
paragraphs: A trained clinician can relocate a kneecap that remains displaced, with suitable pain relief. After assessment and reduction, many first episodes without major associated damage are treated with a temporary support and rehabilitation. Ask exactly whether you may put weight on the leg, how to use crutches and when any brace can be removed or adjusted. A loose piece of bone or cartilage, significant associated injury, marked instability or repeated dislocations may lead to a surgical discussion. Surgery is not automatically necessary after every episode. The operation, potential stiffness, other risks and rehabilitation depend on anatomy, age and the injury, especially in a growing child.

sections.heading: Rehabilitation is a gradual rebuilding process
paragraphs: Once the treating team says it is safe, exercises restore movement, thigh and hip strength, balance and control. Follow the prescribed progression rather than repeatedly testing the knee with twisting or jumping. Ask for pain relief that is suitable for your medicines and health; a cold pack wrapped in cloth can help swelling without freezing the skin. After treatment, elevation when resting may be advised, unlike forcing an unreduced injured knee into a different position. Pain may improve before strength and stability are restored. Returning to sport should depend on function, confidence and the clinician or physiotherapist's assessment, not simply a fixed number of days or the disappearance of swelling.

sections.heading: Follow-up prevents problems from being overlooked
paragraphs: Recovery may take months, and recurrence is possible. Keep follow-up if the knee still gives way, catches, locks, remains swollen or is not regaining movement. Repeated episodes deserve specialist assessment of anatomy and treatment choices rather than indefinite self-management with a support. Seek urgent advice for increasing severe pain, a hot red joint with fever, new numbness or altered foot colour. New calf swelling or pain after reduced mobility also needs prompt assessment; sudden breathlessness or chest pain requires emergency care. Discuss school, work, stairs and transport so that the rehabilitation plan is practical. A child should not be pushed back into sport because an important match is approaching.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: it went back, but still needs checking
examples.text: Lina feels her kneecap slip during a turn. It returns before help arrives, but the knee swells. She seeks assessment rather than resuming play, because a normal-looking position does not exclude internal injury.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: progress before competition
examples.text: Marko walks comfortably after treatment but his knee gives way when changing direction. His physiotherapist adjusts rehabilitation and delays return to football pending reassessment. Walking without pain is useful progress, but does not by itself prove readiness for sport.
